newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU struggles over Helms-Burton peace plan.
newsitem.headline: EU struggles over Helms-Burton peace plan.

text.p: European Union member countries struggled on Wednesday to decide how tough a stance to take against the United States over its anti-Cuba Helms-Burton legislation.

Ambassadors from the 15-nation bloc were meeting in Brussels to discuss a proposed agreement with Washington designed to defuse the transatlantic row over the U.S. law and end a formal dispute panel at the World Trade Organisation (WTO).

Officials said France, Italy, Spain, Belgium and Portugal were insisting that any endorsement of the agreement should be accompanied by a threat to reopen the panel automatically if the United States took any action against EU companies.
Other countries, led by Germany, favour less robust language. The Dutch EU presidency was working on a compromise to be put to the ambassadors later on Wednesday.

The Helms-Burton legislation, an amalgam of U.S. anti-Cuba laws, has outraged Washington's trading partners by threatening various punishments against foreign firms doing certain kinds of business in Cuba.

The row and its resulting WTO panel have strained transatlantic relations and put the WTO disputes procedures to a test that many leading trading countries would like to avoid so early in the organisation's existence.

Under the tentative pact, reached on Friday between Washington and the European Commission, the EU would suspend the panel and the two sides would negotiate a common policy on properties seized by Cuba's communist government after Castro took power in 1959.

They would also work toward a global agreement on protection of expropriated property. The White House would in exchange seek to change a key provision of Helms-Burton barring executives of companies that invest in disputed properties in Cuba from entering the United States.
EU officials said the sensitivity of the issue had been underlined by France, which urged the ambassadors not to talk to journalists about the issue until a decision had been made.
